claim: Computational simulations are subject to statistical fluctuations.
source: Computational simulations, akin to wetlab experimentation, are subject to statistical fluctuations.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental premise in the abstract.

claim: Assigning uncertainties to computed results is of critical importance to drawing statistically reliable conclusions.
source: Assessing the magnitude of these fluctuations, that is, assigning uncertainties to the computed results, is of critical importance to drawing statistically reliable conclusions.
evidence: This is a methodological assertion supported by the examples presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The proposed simulation box size effect disappears with increased sampling in various systems ranging from solvation free energies to protein conformational transition rates.
source: In various systems, ranging from solvation free energies to protein conformational transition rates, we showcase how the proposed simulation box size effect disappears with increased sampling.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by data from multiple systems presented in the results section.

claim: Simulation box size only minimally affects both the thermodynamics and kinetics of the type of biomolecular systems presented in this work.
source: This indicates that, if at all, the simulation box size only minimally affects both the thermodynamics and kinetics of the type of biomolecular systems presented in this work.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comprehensive analysis of multiple systems presented in the results.

claim: Molecular simulations sample well defined thermodynamic ensembles, thus providing a representation of the physical world in silico.
source: Molecular simulations sample well defined thermodynamic ensembles, thus providing a representation of the physical world in silico.
evidence: This is a statement about the fundamental nature of molecular simulations based on established knowledge.

claim: The simulated reality is limited in accuracy by the underlying assumptions and approximations.
source: Naturally, the simulated reality is limited in accuracy by the underlying assumptions and approximations (van Gunsteren and Berendsen, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A frequently noted shortcoming of molecular dynamics simulations is its dependence on the force field.
source: For example, a frequently noted shortcoming of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations is its dependence on the force field, that is, simplified representation of the electronic ground state potential energy.
evidence: This is a well-known limitation in the field.

claim: Large efforts are continuously dedicated to improve force field accuracy.
source: Large efforts are continuously dedicated to improve force field accuracy (Lindorff-Larsen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Sampling convergence is a major simulation accuracy determining factor.
source: Another major simulation accuracy determining factor is the sampling convergence.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle in molecular simulation methodology.

claim: When the phase space is not thoroughly explored, the subsequently estimated thermodynamic and kinetic properties will likely have a substantial associated error.
source: For the cases where the phase space is not thoroughly explored, e.g. relevant protein conformations are not sampled, the subsequently estimated thermodynamic and kinetic properties will likely have a substantial associated error.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of insufficient sampling.

claim: A failure to properly assess error may be critical, leading to an erroneous interpretation of the simulation data and a wrong overall conclusion.
source: A failure to properly assess this error may be critical, leading to an erroneous interpretation of the simulation data and a wrong overall conclusion (Knapp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is a key motivation for the study.

claim: Biomolecular trajectories represent a multidimensional random walk of which the analysis is especially prone to suffer from sampling deficiencies.
source: Considering the stochastic nature of common sampling algorithms such as molecular dynamics simulations, biomolecular trajectories represent a multidimensional random walk of which the analysis is especially prone to suffer from sampling deficiencies (Hess, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Reports have appeared on a possible effect of the simulation box size on thermodynamic quantities in atomistic molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Recently, reports have appeared on a possible effect of the simulation box size on thermodynamic quantities in atomistic molecular dynamics simulations (El Hage et al., 2018; El Hage et al., 2019; Asthagiri and Tomar, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The role of solvation and a box-size-dependent hydrophobic effect have been claimed as the underlying physical cause for box size effects.
source: Specifically, the role of solvation and a box-size-dependent hydrophobic effect have been claimed as the underlying physical cause.
evidence: This summarizes claims from previous studies.

claim: Studies showing no significant box size effects when a larger statistical sample was studied have challenged reports of box size effects.
source: However, these studies have been challenged, showing no significant box size effects when a larger statistical sample was studied (Gapsys and de Groot, 2019; Mehra and Kepp, 2019), indicating a lack of statistical significance of the original results that appeared to show a box size dependence.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: No trend in the computed hydration free energy was observed as a function of the employed simulation box size when all repeats (N = 20) are taken into account for anthracene.
source: As can be seen in Figure 1B, in contrast to Asthagiri and Tomar, 2020, no trend in the computed hydration free energy was observed as a function of the employed simulation box size, when all repeats (N = 20) are taken into account.
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: If relying on single realizations of molecular dynamics trajectories, it is possible to obtain any type of trend suggesting a box size dependence.
source: Naturally, if we were to rely on single realizations of molecular dynamics trajectories, it is possible to obtain any type of trend suggesting a box size dependence: in the middle panel of Figure 1B we highlight an arbitrary selection of an upward, downward, as well as upward followed by downward trends.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1B middle panel.

claim: Trends based on single realizations are not statistically significant and merely illustrate the erroneous conclusion that may be drawn from anecdotal evidence.
source: However, neither trend is statistically significant and merely illustrates the erroneous conclusion that may be drawn from anecdotal evidence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of the data in Figure 1B.

claim: Depicting confidence intervals for the ΔG estimates would help avoiding making unfounded claims about depicted trends.
source: This analysis also clearly illustrates the importance of reporting uncertainty estimates for the calculated observables: depicting confidence intervals for the ΔG estimates (Figure 1B right panel) would help avoiding making unfounded claims about the depicted trends.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the panels in Figure 1B.

claim: The findings on anthracene solvation are well in line with an earlier investigation demonstrating absence of any box size effects in calculating solvation free energies of small neutral molecules.
source: These findings are well in line with an earlier investigation demonstrating absence of any box size effects in calculating solvation free energies of small neutral molecules (Parameswaran and Mobley, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Asthagiri and Tomar, 2020 have reported a box size dependence of a small 56 residue protein GB when computing solvation free energy by means of a quasichemical theory.
source: In fact, Asthagiri and Tomar, 2020 have reported a box size dependence of a small 56 residue protein GB when computing solvation free energy by means of a quasichemical theory.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study.

claim: Switching on protein charges in water appears to be independent of the box size for protein GB.
source: Switching on protein charges in water (Figure 2B left panel) appears to be independent of the box size.
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 2B left panel.

claim: Simulations without solvent for protein GB exhibit strong box size dependence.
source: The simulations without solvent (Figure 2B middle panel) exhibit strong box size dependence.
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 2B middle panel.

claim: The box size dependence in vacuum simulations is explained by the treatment of long range electrostatic interactions using Particle-Mesh-Ewald method with periodic boundaries.
source: The latter result of simulations in vacuum is easy to explain when taking into consideration the treatment of long range electrostatic interactions: in our simulations we followed the nowadays standard approach of Ewald summation (Particle-Mesh-Ewald, PME method [Darden et al., 1993; York et al., 1993]) to account for the electrostatic interactions in a system with periodic boundaries.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the simulation methodology and is supported by citations.

claim: Decreasing the box size in vacuum alters protein's environment, as the distances between the periodic images decrease.
source: Decreasing the box size in vacuum alters protein's environment, as the distances between the periodic images decrease.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of using periodic boundary conditions.

claim: In the solvated system, the electrostatic effect between the periodic images is screened by water molecules.
source: In the solvated system, PME is used as well, but the electrostatic effect between the periodic images is screened by water molecules.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of electrostatic screening in aqueous solutions.

claim: Following best practices of the system setup for molecular dynamics simulations ensures a sufficiently large distance between the periodic images, such that the thermodynamic properties of the system remain box size independent.
source: Following best practices of the system setup for molecular dynamics simulations ensures a sufficiently large distance between the periodic images, such that the thermodynamic properties of the system remain box size independent.
evidence: This is a methodological principle supported by the data presented.

claim: In the current setup for protein GB, the minimal distance between the protein surface and the box edge was at least 1 nm even in the smallest simulation box.
source: For example, in the current setup, the minimal distance between the protein surface and the box edge was at least 1 nm even in the smallest simulation box.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation setup used in the study.

claim: Reducing the box size allowing ∼0.5 nm distance between the solute and the box edge introduces artifacts where water screening is not sufficient and solvation shells of the periodic images can interact with each other.
source: Reducing the box size allowing ∼0.5 nm distance between the solute and the box edge introduces artifacts where water screening is not sufficient and solvation shells of the periodic images can interact with each other.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An extremely small box with ∼0.5 nm distance between the solute and the box edge introduces a clear box size dependence and is not recommended for any MD simulation.
source: Such an extremely small box introduces a clear box size dependence (Figure 3A) and is not recommended for any MD simulation.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and represents a methodological recommendation.

claim: Scaling the charges on water molecules to retain only 10% of the original charge reduces solvent's screening strength making the solvent more similar to a Lennard-Jones fluid.
source: Scaling the charges on water molecules to retain only 10% of the original charge reduces solvent's screening strength making the solvent more similar to a Lennard-Jones fluid.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When water charges are scaled to 10%, the protein's charge introduction free energies become more similar to those in vacuum and a box size dependence emerges.
source: In turn, the protein's charge introduction free energies become more similar to those in vacuum and a box size dependence emerges.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the calculations of ΔGQ for protein GB, no additional corrections were needed, while Asthagiri and Tomar used an analytical correction to remove box size dependence.
source: Also, it is worth noting that in our calculations of ΔGQ we did not need to apply any additional corrections, while Asthagiri and Tomar used an analytical correction (Hummer et al., 1998) to remove box size dependence of this ΔG component.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: The need for analytical correction to remove box size dependence might depend on the particular details how the MD software computes the solvation free energy.
source: The need for such a correction might depend on the particular details how the MD software computes the solvation free energy.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the comparison with previous work.

claim: Gromacs considers all the terms, including short and long range solute-solvent, solute-solute, as well as self interactions in solvation free energy calculations.
source: Gromacs (Abraham et al., 2015), the simulation package used in this work, considers all the terms, including short and long range solute-solvent, solute-solute, as well as self interactions.
evidence: This is a description of the software implementation, supported by a citation.

claim: There is a large discrepancy between the estimated absolute value of the ΔGQ component reported by Asthagiri and Tomar (−662 kcal/mol) and the current work (−994 kcal/mol).
source: Another marked difference between the calculation reported by Asthagiri and Tomar and our work comes from the estimated absolute value of the ΔGQ component: −662 kcal/mol and −994 kcal/mol, respectively.
evidence: This is a comparison of numerical results between studies.

claim: The calculation of the solvation free energy of a whole protein is a highly specific endeavour, thus the absolute value of the estimated ΔG will strongly depend on the particular details of the simulation setup.
source: The calculation of the solvation free energy of a whole protein is a highly specific endeavour, thus the absolute value of the estimated ΔG will strongly depend on the particular details of the simulation setup.
evidence: This is a general principle about protein solvation free energy calculations.

claim: Asthagiri and Tomar chose to freeze all the degrees of freedom of the protein to facilitate convergence and avoid protein unfolding for the simulations in vacuum.
source: To facilitate convergence and avoid protein unfolding for the simulations in vacuum Asthagiri and Tomar chose to freeze all the degrees of freedom of the protein.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in a previous study.

claim: In the current study's setup for protein GB, protein motions were only restricted by harmonic position restraints.
source: In our setup we only restricted the protein motions by harmonic position restraints.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the current study.

claim: Having all the protein degrees of freedom constrained (or restrained) exaggerates the influence of the starting structure for simulation as the internal dynamics of the solute is restricted and the solvent will interact with the initial conformer only.
source: An even larger contribution to the discrepancy can be expected from having all the protein degrees of freedom constrained (or restrained), as it exaggerates the influence of the starting structure for simulation: the internal dynamics of the solute is restricted and the solvent will interact with the initial conformer only.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of different restraint protocols.

claim: Proper equilibration of water molecules was performed for the solvation free energy calculations of protein GB by using Hamiltonian replica exchange simulations.
source: Another aspect that we took particular care of was to properly equilibrate water molecules for the solvation free energy calculations. In the first step we performed annihilation of the van der Waals interactions of uncharged GB using Hamiltonian replica exchange simulations.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in the current study.

claim: Exhaustive equilibration allowed water molecules to explore deep pockets of the protein, later contributing to the final free energy estimate for protein GB.
source: Naturally, such an exhaustive equilibration allowed water molecules to explore deep pockets of the protein, later contributing to the final free energy estimate.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of the equilibration protocol.

claim: A considerable amount of sampling is required to reach convergence for an alchemical solvation of the whole protein, as the phase space overlap between neighboring windows needs to be ensured.
source: Lastly, a considerable amount of sampling is required to reach convergence for an alchemical solvation of the whole protein, as the phase space overlap between neighboring windows needs to be ensured.
evidence: This is a general principle about alchemical free energy calculations.

claim: 1.38 μs of sampling was invested for the ΔGQ solvation in water for each box size including sampling enhancement by means of Hamiltonian replica exchange for protein GB.
source: In this work we invested 1.38 μs of sampling for the ΔGQ solvation in water for each box size including sampling enhancement by means of Hamiltonian replica exchange.
evidence: This is a description of the computational effort in the current study.

claim: Considering different sampling times in this work and that reported by Asthagiri and Tomar might further contribute to the discrepancy in the estimated ΔGQ values.
source: Considering different sampling times in this work and that reported by Asthagiri and Tomar might further contribute to the discrepancy in the estimated ΔGQ values.
evidence: This is a speculation about the source of discrepancy between studies.

claim: No box size dependence is present neither in the solvated, nor in the vacuum state for the van der Waals interaction contribution to the solvation free energy of protein GB.
source: As for the van der Waals interaction contribution to the solvation free energy, no box size dependence is present neither in the solvated, nor in the vacuum state (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The box-size dependence for hydration free energies as reported by Asthagiri and Tomar, 2020 is not a general phenomenon but a feature of the applied quasichemical theory.
source: This result shows that the box-size dependence for hydration free energies as reported by Asthagiri and Tomar, 2020 is not a general phenomenon but a feature of the applied quasichemical theory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of results using different methods.

claim: Both the anthracene and protein G van der Waals coupling examples address the hydration free energy of a hydrophobic molecule and serve to test the hypothesis of a possible box size dependence of the hydrophobic effect.
source: It is of interest to note that both the anthracene and protein G van der Waals coupling examples address the hydration free energy of a hydrophobic molecule. Hence, these also serve to test the hypothesis of a possible box size dependence of the hydrophobic effect, as had been suggested (El Hage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the significance of the results, with a citation to previous work.

claim: The current series of studies do not provide any evidence that the solvation-driven hydrophobic effect is significantly affected by solvation beyond the first solvation layers.
source: Even though according to one theory of hydrophobicity the anthracene and protein G cases are relatively small systems (Chandler, 2005), the current series do not provide any evidence that the solvation-driven hydrophobic effect is significantly affected by solvation beyond the first solvation layers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data, with a citation to a theory of hydrophobicity.

claim: Limited sampling (e.g. 0.1% of the data) for alanine dipeptide may lead to erroneous conclusions about the box size-dependent ratio between the alanine dipeptide conformers.
source: Also here, limited sampling, e.g. 0.1% of the data, may lead to erroneous conclusions about the box size-dependent ratio between the alanine dipeptide conformers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The discrepancies between the free energy profiles generated in different simulation boxes for alanine dipeptide disappear with more sampling data included.
source: The discrepancies between the free energy profiles generated in different simulation boxes disappear with more sampling data included.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Babu and Lim, 2020 reported a strongly box size-dependent potential of mean force profile for the M20 loop motion of dihydrofolate reductase.
source: Babu and Lim, 2020 reported a strongly box size-dependent potential of mean force (PMF) profile for the M20 loop motion (Figure 5B) of the protein.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the study by Babu and Lim, the protein dihydrofolate reductase was solvated in three cubic boxes of varying size (box edge length of 7, 8 and 9.3 nm).
source: In their study, the protein was solvated in three cubic boxes of varying size (box edge length of 7, 8 and 9.3 nm).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used in a previous study.

claim: Even the smallest box used by Babu and Lim was sufficient to avoid protein self interactions (minimal distance between periodic images at least 1.4 nm).
source: Even the smallest box was sufficient to avoid protein self interactions (minimal distance between periodic images at least 1.4 nm).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation setup in a previous study.

claim: Babu and Lim reported the PMF profile in the smallest box to deviate significantly from the other two larger boxes for dihydrofolate reductase.
source: In spite of this apparently sufficient solvation, the authors have reported the PMF profile in the smallest box to deviate significantly from the other two larger boxes.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study.

claim: The free energy profiles for dihydrofolate reductase obtained from simulations of 2.5 ns (with 0.5 ns discarded for equilibration) show an apparent box size dependence.
source: Indeed, the free energy profiles obtained from these simulations show an apparent box size dependence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5C upper panel.

claim: In contrast to the original finding by Babu and Lim, it was the middle box (8 nm edge length) that showed a different behaviour for dihydrofolate reductase in the short simulations.
source: However, in contrast to the original finding, it was the middle box (8 nm edge length) that showed a different behaviour, which appears statistically significant within the limited sampling at hand.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5C upper panel.

claim: The profiles for dihydrofolate reductase obtained from 50 ns simulations (after discarding the first 10 ns from each window for equilibration) are statistically indistinguishable among the different box sizes.
source: The profiles obtained from these simulations, after discarding the first 10 ns from each window for equilibration, are statistically indistinguishable among the different box sizes (Figure 5C bottom panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5C bottom panel.

claim: For the shorter distances in dihydrofolate reductase simulations, autocorrelations significantly larger than zero persist for up to 10 ns.
source: For the shorter distances (for brevity, in the figure we show the data for seven windows only), we observe autocorrelations significantly larger than zero pertaining for up to 10 ns.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The autocorrelations from the short 2.5 ns dihydrofolate reductase simulations follow different trends and are significantly different from those obtained from the longer 50 ns runs.
source: The autocorrelations from the short 2.5 ns simulations follow different trends and are significantly different from those obtained from the longer 50 ns runs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Analyzing the autocorrelations from the short trajectories may lead to the impression that the 2.5 ns simulation is readily converged, as the local free energy minimum is properly sampled and the trajectory appears to be memoryless.
source: It is evident that analyzing the autocorrelations from the short trajectories may lead to the impression that the 2.5 ns simulation is readily converged, as the local free energy minimum is properly sampled and the trajectory appears to be memoryless.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of autocorrelation data.

claim: It is only possible to deduce that a simulation is not converged after obtaining a better converged simulation.
source: Unfortunately, this situation reveals the nature of the problem being akin to that of Zeno's paradoxes (Aristotle, 350BC, Physics, Book VI): it is only possible to deduce that a simulation is not converged after obtaining a better converged simulation.
evidence: This is a philosophical observation about the nature of convergence assessment, with a citation to Aristotle.

claim: The longer trajectories for dihydrofolate reductase reveal that there are other relevant free energy minima, the sampling of which uncovers longer autocorrelation times and subsequently has a pronounced effect on the free energy profiles.
source: The longer trajectories reveal that there are other relevant free energy minima, the sampling of which uncovers longer autocorrelation times and subsequently has a pronounced effect on the free energy profiles.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of short and long simulations.

claim: The free energy profiles for dihydrofolate reductase obtained from the trajectories of 10 ns already show that the average values for the three box sizes approach one another and the remaining differences are largely within the range of uncertainty.
source: The free energy profiles obtained from the trajectories of 10 ns (Figure 5C middle panel) already show that the average values for the three box sizes approach one another and the remaining differences are largely within the range of uncertainty.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5C middle panel.

claim: The dihydrofolate reductase case illustrates the importance of generating independent samples and taking into account autocorrelation times to obtain unbiased estimates.
source: Furthermore, this case illustrates the importance of generating independent samples and taking into account autocorrelation times to obtain unbiased estimates.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion drawn from the analysis.

claim: For the dihydrofolate reductase profiles, 95% confidence intervals from three independent repeats erroneously indicated statistically significant difference between the simulation boxes when using short simulations.
source: For the profiles and associated uncertainties in Figure 5C (upper panel), 95% confidence intervals from three independent repeats erroneously indicated statistically signifcant difference between the simulation boxes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5C upper panel.

claim: The under-estimation of the standard error for dihydrofolate reductase appears due to remaining dependence between the three repeats, as they all started from the same initial structure.
source: This under-estimation of the standard error appears due to remaining dependence between the three repeats, as they all started from the same initial structure.
evidence: This is an inference about the source of error in the statistical analysis.

claim: The short overall sampling time with a brief equilibration phase for dihydrofolate reductase were insufficient to remove autocorrelations at longer time-scales.
source: The short overall sampling time with a brief equilibration phase were insufficient to remove autocorrelations at longer time-scales.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: The sufficient equilibration time is system dependent.
source: The sufficient equilibration time is system dependent: as we showed before in Figure 4C, for alanine dipeptide even shorter simulations were sufficient to obtain reliable error estimates.
evidence: This is a general principle illustrated by comparing different systems.

claim: For the same simulation system, differences in transition times between single repeats have been reported and interpreted.
source: For the same simulation system, differences in transition times between single repeats have been reported and interpreted (El Hage et al., 2018) while at the same time it has been argued that hundreds to thousands of transitions should be sampled for an estimate of kinetic rate constants (El Hage et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a citation to previous studies showing inconsistent approaches.

claim: It has been argued that hundreds to thousands of transitions should be sampled for an estimate of kinetic rate constants.
source: For the same simulation system, differences in transition times between single repeats have been reported and interpreted (El Hage et al., 2018) while at the same time it has been argued that hundreds to thousands of transitions should be sampled for an estimate of kinetic rate constants (El Hage et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study.

claim: Although sampling only ten transitions for alanine dipeptide provides a rather sparse distribution of the transition times, no systematic effect on the rate estimate was observed.
source: Although sampling only ten transitions provides a rather sparse distribution of the transition times (Figure 6A), no systematic effect on the rate estimate was observed (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: The effect of statistics on alanine dipeptide transition rate estimates solely manifests itself in the uncertainty of the rate estimate.
source: Rather, the effect of statistics in this case solely manifests itself in the uncertainty of the rate estimate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: To resolve the question of how many transitions are required for a rate estimate, it depends on the required precision for the question at hand.
source: Thus, to resolve the question of how many transitions are required for a rate estimate, it depends on the required precision for the question at hand.
evidence: This is a general principle about statistical estimation.

claim: For an order of magnitude estimate of transition rates, a single transition time may be sufficient.
source: For an order of magnitude estimate, a single transition time may be sufficient, whereas multiple repeats are necessary to obtain a higher precision.
evidence: This is a general principle about statistical estimation.

claim: Multiple repeats are necessary to obtain a higher precision for transition rate estimates.
source: For an order of magnitude estimate, a single transition time may be sufficient, whereas multiple repeats are necessary to obtain a higher precision.
evidence: This is a general principle about statistical estimation.

claim: For the general case there is not a single rule of thumb for the required number of repeats for transition rate estimates.
source: Thus, for the general case there is not a single rule of thumb for the required number of repeats.
evidence: This is a general principle about statistical estimation.

claim: The original discussion on a possible box size dependence in biomolecular simulations was prompted by an investigation into quaternary transitions in human hemoglobin.
source: The original discussion on a possible box size dependence in biomolecular simulations was prompted by an investigation into quaternary transitions in human hemoglobin, where in apo simulations of the protein, spontaneous transitions from the T to the R state were observed and an effect of the simulation box size on the transition probability was reported (El Hage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study.

claim: In apo simulations of hemoglobin, spontaneous transitions from the T to the R state were observed and an effect of the simulation box size on the transition probability was reported.
source: The original discussion on a possible box size dependence in biomolecular simulations was prompted by an investigation into quaternary transitions in human hemoglobin, where in apo simulations of the protein, spontaneous transitions from the T to the R state were observed and an effect of the simulation box size on the transition probability was reported (El Hage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study.

claim: For all studied box sizes of hemoglobin, some repeats were found to make the transition to R state, whereas other repeats were found to remain closer to T state.
source: For all studied box sizes, some repeats were found to make the transition, defined as ending up closer to the R state, whereas other repeats were found to remain closer to T.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: If only one repeat per case had been carried out for hemoglobin, all scenarios about which box sizes show transitions could be picked with a substantial probability.
source: Although the conclusion that the transition can take place in all three box sizes (consistent with the obervations from all 21 repeats) represents the most probable case also all other scenarios could be picked with a substantial probability, illustrating the risk of working with N = 1 statistics.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: For hemoglobin, no significant differences between the studied box sizes are observed for any number of repeats in the frequentist analysis.
source: For the data at hand, no significant differences between the studied box sizes are observed for any number of repeats.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The null hypothesis that all hemoglobin samples were drawn from the same distribution cannot be rejected in the frequentist analysis.
source: Hence, the null hypothesis that all samples were drawn from the same distribution cannot be rejected.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the frequentist statistical analysis.

claim: The hypothesis that the T to R transition time in hemoglobin is affected by the simulation box size is not supported by the data in the frequentist analysis.
source: Accordingly, the hypothesis that the T to R transition time is affected by the simulation box size is not supported by the data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the frequentist statistical analysis.

claim: The frequentist inference based hypothesis testing only concludes that there is no sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis, but does not allow one to quantify the statistical significance of the opposite.
source: The frequentist inference based hypothesis testing, as formulated above, only concludes that there is no sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. It does not, however, allow one to quantify the statistical significance of the opposite, that is, that the kinetics of hemoglobin in differently sized boxes are governed by one process.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of frequentist inference.

claim: Bayesian inference allows making quantitative statements about the rates when only one or even no transitions are observed throughout a simulation.
source: Another advantage of the Bayesian approach is that it allows making quantitative statements about the rates when only one or even no transitions are observed throughout a simulation.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of Bayesian inference.

claim: The choice of prior has a large influence on the probability distribution for the rate for single simulations of hemoglobin, but this effect is much smaller for 10, 20 and 100 repeats.
source: As shown in Figure 9, whereas the choice of prior has a large influence on the probability distribution for the rate for single simulations, this effect is much smaller for 10, 20 and 100 repeats.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 9.

claim: For a Bayes factor (odds ratio) of around one, no distinction can be made and both samples might have been drawn either from the same or two different distributions.
source: For a Bayes factor (odds ratio) of around one, no distinction can be made and both samples might have been drawn either from the same or two different distributions.
evidence: This is a principle of Bayesian inference illustrated by the data in Figure 10.

claim: For Bayes factors in the range between 0.33 and 3, Jeffreys has suggested the label 'barely worth mentioning' as no distinction can be made between a single or different distributions.
source: For Bayes factors in this range between 0.33 and 3 Jeffreys has suggested the label ''barely worth mentioning'' as no distinction can be made between a single or different distributions.
evidence: This is a citation to Jeffreys' interpretation of Bayes factors.

claim: For a Bayes factor of less than 0.33, there is strong evidence that both samples were drawn from a single distribution.
source: For a Bayes factor of less than 0.33, there is strong evidence that both samples were drawn from a single distribution.
evidence: This is a principle of Bayesian inference illustrated by the data in Figure 10.

claim: A Bayes factor larger than three would strongly indicate that two different distributions were underlying the samples.
source: The third scenario of Bayes factor larger than three would strongly indicate that two different distributions were underlying the samples.
evidence: This is a principle of Bayesian inference illustrated by the data in Figure 10.

claim: All comparisons of different box sizes involving single simulation repeats of hemoglobin result in Bayes factors of close to one, meaning that for the associated cases it cannot be distinguished if they stem from a single or two different distributions.
source: All comparisons of different box sizes involving single simulation repeats (first three rows of Table 1) result in Bayes factors of close to one, meaning that for the associated cases it cannot be distinguished if they stem from a single or two different distributions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Table 1.

claim: For hemoglobin comparisons of 9 vs 12 nm, 9 vs 15 nm and 12 vs 15 nm with higher simulation repeat numbers, there is substantial evidence that these samples were drawn from a single distribution.
source: Whereas for 9 vs 12 nm and 9 vs 15 nm the outcome remains ambiguous for N = 10,20, for the remaining cases of 9 vs 12 nm, 9 vs 15 nm and 12 vs 15 nm, the suggested interpretation from Jeffreys, 1961; Kass and Raftery, 1995 is that there is substantial evidence that these samples were drawn from a single distribution.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Table 1 and is based on the interpretation framework from cited sources.

claim: There is an important difference between Bayes factor categories: the category with Bayes factors between 0.33 and 3 indicate insufficient evidence to justify a conclusion of a box size effect but there might still be such an effect, while cases with Bayes factor of 0.33 or lower provide substantial evidence that all transition times were drawn from a single distribution.
source: Please note that there is an important difference between these two classes in their implications. Whereas the category with Bayes factors with values between 0.33 and 3 indicate that there is insufficient evidence to justify a conclusion of a box size effect, there might still be such an effect. The three cases with higher simulation repeat numbers (Table 1) with a Bayes factor of 0.33 or lower in fact provide substantial evidence that all transition times were drawn from a single distribution, thus providing evidence that the simulation box size does not affect the transition time of the T to R transition in hemoglobin.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian analysis results shown in Table 1.

claim: There are well documented cases in the literature demonstrating and explaining the underlying reasons of box size effects on water dynamics.
source: For the water dynamics, however, there are well documented cases in the literature demonstrating and explaining the underlying reasons of the box size effects.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: A small effect on the diffusion of bulk water is observed due to periodic boundary effects, as described by Yeh and Hummer, 2004.
source: A small effect on the diffusion of bulk water is observed due to periodic boundary effects, as described by Yeh and Hummer, 2004.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and is demonstrated in Figure 11B.

claim: Applying a hydrodynamic correction derived by Yeh and Hummer removes any box size effect on the diffusion coefficient in bulk water.
source: Applying a hydrodynamic correction derived by Yeh and Hummer removes any box size effect on the diffusion coefficient in bulk water.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and is demonstrated in Figure 11B.

claim: A much stronger effect on the water diffusion constant is observed when a large protein (hemoglobin) is added to the simulation box.
source: A much stronger effect on the water diffusion constant is observed when a large protein, in this case hemoglobin, is added to the simulation box (square symbols).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: The apparent strong box size effect on water diffusion in hemoglobin simulations manifests due to the fact that only little bulk water (capable of diffusing with the bulk-like diffusion constant) is present in the smaller boxes.
source: The apparent strong box size effect manifests due to the fact that only little bulk water (capable of diffusing with the bulk-like diffusion constant) is present in the smaller boxes.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed effect, supported by the analysis in Figure 11.

claim: After renormalizing the smaller hemoglobin boxes to the level of 15 nm box by employing the value of bulk water diffusion weighted by the difference in the number of water molecules, the original strong effect from the straight averages has vanished.
source: As can be seen in Figure 11B (circles), the original strong effect from the straight averages (squares) has vanished, indicating that the original apparent effect was largely dominated by a normalization artifact arising from a difference in protein-to-water ratio.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: The original apparent box size effect on water diffusion in hemoglobin simulations was largely dominated by a normalization artifact arising from a difference in protein-to-water ratio.
source: As can be seen in Figure 11B (circles), the original strong effect from the straight averages (squares) has vanished, indicating that the original apparent effect was largely dominated by a normalization artifact arising from a difference in protein-to-water ratio.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis shown in Figure 11B.

claim: There is a remaining small trend in water diffusion after normalization, and it will be interesting to analyze in the future if this stems from the crude extrapolation procedure or if it reflects an effect of the periodic boundary conditions.
source: It should be noted that the applied extrapolation procedure is approximate, as here we have used simple averaging of non-corrected diffusion coefficients. There is a remaining small trend visible and it will be interesting to analyze in the future if this stems from our crude extrapolation procedure or if it reflects an effect of the periodic boundary conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of the remaining trend.

claim: A straightforward analysis of solvent radial distribution function is complicated by normalization issues, which can lead to artifacts when comparing boxes of different size.
source: As with the diffusion constant, a straightforward analysis such as a solvent radial distribution function (RDF) is complicated by normalization issues, which can lead to artifacts when comparing boxes of different size (El Hage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The issue with RDF normalization arises due to the fact that RDF is normalized by the particle density in the box, and in a realistic simulation box, a fraction of its volume that is occupied by the protein is not accessible to water.
source: The issue arises due to the fact that RDF is normalized by the particle density (in the current case, water density) in the box. In an infinitely diluted system, the density would approach the value of bulk water. In a realistic simulation box, however, a fraction of its volume that is occupied by the protein is not accessible to water.
evidence: This is an explanation of the normalization issue based on the definition of RDF.

claim: The calculated RDF is larger than the true RDF by Vbox/(Vbox-Vprotein), and this ratio depends on the box size, making the normalization of RDF box size-dependent.
source: This way, the calculated RDF is larger than the true RDF by Vbox/(Vbox-Vprotein). This ratio depends on the box size, in turn, making the normalization of RDF box size-dependent.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the normalization procedure.

claim: A previous analysis showed that the strong apparent box size effect on the solvent RDF initially derived from the different box sizes vanished upon consistent normalization.
source: This analysis showed that the strong apparent box size effect on the solvent RDF initially derived from the different box sizes (El Hage et al., 2018) vanished upon consistent normalization (Gapsys and de Groot, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The result of spherical RDF normalization is consistent with previous observations and confirms that no significant box size effects are observed in terms of protein solvation and, by implication, the hydrophobic effect.
source: As can be seen in Figure 11C, the result of this radial normalization is consistent with our previous observation (Gapsys and de Groot, 2019) as well as the anthracene solvation presented in Figure 1 and it confirms that no significant box size effects are observed in terms of protein solvation and, by implication, the hydrophobic effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 11C and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: The combined results demonstrate the established mild box size dependence of bulk water dynamics.
source: The combined results from Figure 11 demonstrate the established (Yeh and Hummer, 2004) mild box size dependence of bulk water dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis in Figure 11, supported by a citation.

claim: No evidence for a thermodynamic effect on the solvent shell was found.
source: In contrast, no evidence for a thermodynamic effect on the solvent shell was found.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RDF analysis.

claim: No statistically significant box size effects on the kinetics and thermodynamics of biomolecules were observed in this work.
source: In the work we have not observed any statistically significant box size effects on the kinetics and thermodynamics of biomolecules.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the data presented.

claim: All box sizes studied in this work included a solvent shell of at least 1 nm in size, or at least three solvation layers between the studied biomolecule and the box edge.
source: It should be noted, however, that all box sizes studied in this work included a solvent shell of at least 1 nm in size, or at least three solvation layers between the studied biomolecule and the box edge.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation setup used in the study.

claim: Beyond a distance of 1 nm between the biomolecule and the box edge, only minimal box size effects should be expected.
source: Beyond that range only minimal box size effects should be expected, as shown, but naturally box size artifacts may occur for smaller boxes due to (indirect) self-interaction caused by the periodic nature of typical molecular dynamics boxes (van Gunsteren and Berendsen, 1990; Mehra and Kepp, 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data, supported by citations.

claim: Box size artifacts may occur for smaller boxes due to (indirect) self-interaction caused by the periodic nature of typical molecular dynamics boxes.
source: Beyond that range only minimal box size effects should be expected, as shown, but naturally box size artifacts may occur for smaller boxes due to (indirect) self-interaction caused by the periodic nature of typical molecular dynamics boxes (van Gunsteren and Berendsen, 1990; Mehra and Kepp, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The box-size independence demonstrated in this work is limited to box sizes that exceed a distance of 1 nm between the biomolecule and the box edge.
source: Therefore the box-size independence demonstrated in this work is limited to box sizes that exceed a distance of 1 nm between the biomolecule and the box edge.
evidence: This is a limitation of the conclusions drawn from the study.

claim: Simulations in particularly small boxes may have a profound effect on the lateral lipid diffusion, resulting in significant correlations in lipid motions.
source: Similarly, simulations in particularly small boxes may have a profound effect on the lateral lipid diffusion, resulting in significant correlations in lipid motions (Klauda et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Lateral diffusion of lipids, as well as membrane proteins embedded in a lipid bilayer depend on the simulation box size and box asymmetry due to the hydrodynamic effects.
source: Furthermore, lateral diffusion of lipids, as well as membrane proteins embedded in a lipid bilayer depend on the simulation box size and box asymmetry due to the hydrodynamic effects (Vögele et al., 2018),
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Hydrodynamic effects also induce the rotational diffusion dependence on the simulation box size.
source: Hydrodynamic effects also induce the rotational diffusion dependence on the simulation box size (Linke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Analytical hydrodynamic corrections for lateral and rotational diffusion effects have been proposed.
source: Analytical hydrodynamic corrections for the latter effects have been proposed (Vögele and Hummer, 2016; Linke et al., 2018) in a similar fashion to the correction for the bulk water diffusion by Yeh and Hummer, 2004.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For a charged simulation box, a uniformly distributed neutralizing background charge will be introduced automatically by the Ewald methods.
source: For a charged simulation box, a uniformly distributed neutralizing background charge will be introduced automatically by the Ewald methods, thus the charges in the simulated system will experience a potential which will depend on the solvent volume (Lin et al., 2014) and dielectric constants of the solvents (Hub et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The charges in a charged simulation system will experience a potential which will depend on the solvent volume and dielectric constants of the solvents.
source: For a charged simulation box, a uniformly distributed neutralizing background charge will be introduced automatically by the Ewald methods, thus the charges in the simulated system will experience a potential which will depend on the solvent volume (Lin et al., 2014) and dielectric constants of the solvents (Hub et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Posthoc corrections to the free energies calculated in the charged periodic systems exist.
source: While posthoc corrections to the free energies calculated in the charged periodic systems exist (Rocklin et al., 2013; Hub et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2014; Reif and Oostenbrink, 2014), a generalize advice to obtaining reliable dynamic trajectories would be, if possible, to neutralize the simulation system.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A generalized advice to obtaining reliable dynamic trajectories would be, if possible, to neutralize the simulation system.
source: While posthoc corrections to the free energies calculated in the charged periodic systems exist (Rocklin et al., 2013; Hub et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2014; Reif and Oostenbrink, 2014), a generalize advice to obtaining reliable dynamic trajectories would be, if possible, to neutralize the simulation system.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the discussion of charged systems.

claim: A reliable uncertainty estimation is not a mere nuisance, but an essential part of good scientific practice.
source: All in all, in the work we aimed at collecting a comprehensive set of examples illustrating that a reliable uncertainty estimation is not a mere nuisance, but an essential part of good scientific practice.
evidence: This is a key message of the study.

claim: Ignoring to obtain error estimates and relying on single realizations of processes stochastic in nature may lead to drawing incorrect conclusions.
source: Ignoring to obtain error estimates and relying on single realizations of processes stochastic in nature may lead to drawing incorrect conclusions, as for example showcased in Figure 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the examples in the manuscript, particularly Figure 1.

claim: A previous work by El Hage et al., 2018 serves as clear illustration of drawing incorrect conclusions when interpreting a set of single (no replicas) simulation trajectories.
source: A previous work by El Hage et al., 2018 serves as clear illustration of this when interpreting a set of single (no replicas) simulation trajectories.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous study that is critiqued in the current work.

claim: Upon generation of a larger data sample, the previous conclusions of El Hage et al. are shown not to hold.
source: Upon generation of a larger data sample, the previous conclusions of El Hage et al. are shown not to hold (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Due to the stochastic nature of most commonly used sampling integrators, it is of critical importance that sampling convergence is demonstrated.
source: Due to the stochastic nature of most commonly used sampling integrators, it is of critical importance that sampling convergence is demonstrated.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of molecular simulation methodology.

claim: Sampling convergence can be achieved in single runs if the slowest degree of freedom relevant for the property of interest is reversibly sampled multiple times.
source: This can be achieved in single runs if the slowest degree of freedom relevant for the property of interest is reversibly sampled multiple times.
evidence: This is a methodological principle about assessing convergence.

claim: Multiple repeats can be carried out to check for reproducibility and convergence.
source: Alternatively, multiple repeats can be carried out to check for reproducibility and convergence.
evidence: This is a methodological principle about assessing convergence.

claim: The use of multiple repeats has many additional advantages such as a straightforward error estimate obtained from the spread among individual repeats.
source: The use of multiple repeats has many additional advantages such as a straightforward error estimate obtained from the spread among individual repeats.
evidence: This is a methodological principle about statistical analysis.

claim: A practical advantage of multiple repeats is its trivial parallelization.
source: A practical advantage of multiple repeats is its trivial parallelization.
evidence: This is a practical consideration about computational implementation.

claim: In the absence of multiple repeats, there is a substantial risk of lack of reproducibility due to the fact that the results from individual runs may have happened by chance and are not representative of a larger set.
source: In the absence of multiple repeats, there is a substantial risk of lack of reproducibility due to the fact that the results from individual runs may have happened by chance and are not representative of a larger set.
evidence: This is a general principle about statistical reliability.

claim: Anecdotal evidence may be useful for hypothesis generation but should be followed up by a more thorough statistical approach.
source: Such anecdotal evidence may be useful for hypothesis generation but should be followed up by a more thorough statistical approach.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation about scientific practice.

claim: An initial indication of an apparent box size effect in molecular dynamics simulations based on single repeats was not confirmed when repeated with an order of magnitude more statistics.
source: The examples provided in this work illustrate that an initial indication of an apparent box size effect in molecular dynamics simulations based on single repeats was not confirmed when repeated with an order of magnitude more statistics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the data presented.
